newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban prepare defence of Kabul after reverses.
newsitem.headline: Taleban prepare defence of Kabul after reverses.

text.p: The Afghan Taleban militia was preparing the defence of Kabul on Monday after suffering stunning reverses north of the city at the hands of the government it ousted less than three weeks ago, witnesses said.

They said the purist Islamic militia, which had swept all before it until coming up against the wall of the Hindu Kush, was reinforcing positions on the two roads north of the capital and one entering the city from the west.
A large force of Taleban was assembling about 20 km (12 miles) north of Kabul to block the main road from the north and moving artillery and other weapoons to block the second road, they said.

Some 60 tanks were massed outside Kabul on the main road from the west, apparently to block any attempt by the forces of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood to make a flanking attack, the witnesses added.
Masood's forces have swept the Taleban a long way back from their former front line, at Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass going through the Hindu Kush, in the past two days.

Less than a week after being besieged in his Panjsher Valley fortress, a two-hour drive north of Kabul, and apparently fighting to survive, Masood has pushed the Taleban much of the way back to Kabul.
He took Jabal os-Siraj on Saturday and then pushed the Taleban out of Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south, later in the day after a fierce five-hour battle.

It was not clear how far south of Charikar his largely ethnic Tajik forces had pushed or whether Masood intended to attack Kabul, the city he left without a fight on September 27 in the face of a lightning push by the Taleban.
But witnesses said the town of Qarah Bagh, on the road about a third of the way between Charikar and Kabul, was deserted and the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban were massed nearby.
They said it appeared the Taleban controlled little more than the roads after Masood sent guerrilla bands behind the front lines.
Other groups, which had joined the Taleban as they took Kabul, had switched sides again and had cut the road below Qarah Bagh, the witnesses said.

"It seems the cutting of the road there and Masood ambushes behind the lines at Jabal os-Siraj prevented reinforcements and ammunition reaching the Taleban up there," said one Afghan-watcher in Kabul.
Masood's guerrilla bands also appear to have isolated Taleban forces at Bagram, the government's main air base 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital.
Taleban fighters in the area said on Sunday the guerrillas had moved south of the air base and the road from it to Kabul had been closed to civilian traffic.
There has been no word from Masood on what he plans next after his victories, and with the well-armed Taleban showing no signs of giving up Kabul, Afghan-watchers said the future was uncertain.

"Many people here think Masood gave up Kabul to spare the people another battle for the city and that he still would not want to inflict another on them," said one Afghan-watcher in a city partially destroyed in factional fighting over the past four years.
"It may be that with the Taleban losing confidence, there may be an opportunity for peace talks," he said.

Powerful northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, who runs six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces from Mazar-i-Sharif north of the Hindu Kush, signed a pact with Masood last week promising to join him unless the Taleban stopped fighting.
However, he has said consistently he prefers talks, as have the Taleban, and there is no evidence yet of Uzbek help to Masood on the ground.
"But we are not hearing any serious sounds about talks and from here, anything could happen," the Afghan-watcher said.
